concepts.title: Producers and Consumers
concepts.explanation:
You know that a plant makes its own food using sunlight, and that an animal cannot. Put those two facts side by side and you have the most useful idea in biology.

A plant is a producer. It produces its own food out of sunlight, water and air, and it needs no other living thing to feed it.

An animal is a consumer. It consumes - it eats - because it cannot make food inside itself. Every animal, including you, must eat something that was once alive.

Now follow the food. Grass is a producer. A goat eats the grass, so the goat is a consumer. A person drinks the goat's milk or eats its meat, so the person is a consumer too. Write it with arrows and you have a food chain:

grass → goat → person

The arrow means 'is eaten by', and it also shows which way the food is travelling. Every food chain starts with a producer, because nothing else can make food out of sunlight. Take the grass away and the whole chain has nothing to stand on.

Here is another: maize → chicken → person. And another from the sea: tiny sea plants → small fish → big fish.

Count the producers in each one. There is always exactly one, and it is always first.
concepts.example: Think of a meal you ate today. Write a food chain of three links that ends with you, and put the arrows the right way round. Then say which link is the producer, and how you know.

concepts.title: The Groups of Animals
concepts.explanation:
There are far too many kinds of animal to learn one at a time, so scientists sort them into groups. Animals in the same group share features you can check.

Fish live in water all their lives. They have scales, they breathe through gills, and they lay eggs in the water. A tilapia is a fish.

Amphibians begin life in water and move onto land. They have smooth, damp skin, and they lay their eggs in water. A frog is an amphibian - a tadpole in water first, then a frog that can sit on the bank.

Reptiles have dry, scaly skin, and they lay eggs with tough shells on land. A lizard, a snake, a tortoise and a crocodile are reptiles.

Birds have feathers, two wings, a beak and no teeth, and they lay hard-shelled eggs. A hen, a crow and an ostrich are all birds, even the ones that cannot fly.

Mammals have hair or fur, and the mothers feed their young on milk. A goat, a bat, a whale and you are all mammals.

The quickest way to place an animal is to ask about its covering: scales in water, damp skin, dry scales, feathers, or hair. That one question sorts most animals you will meet.
concepts.example: Name one animal you have seen from three different groups. For each one, say which feature told you the group - the covering, where it lays its eggs, or how it feeds its young.

concepts.title: How Young Animals Grow Up
concepts.explanation:
Every animal grows from young to adult, but they do not all take the same road.

Some young are small copies of their parents. A kid looks like a little goat from the day it is born - four legs, hooves, the same shape - and it simply gets bigger and stronger. A chick is a small bird that grows proper feathers and becomes a hen. This is the straightforward road, and it is the one mammals and birds take.

Other young look nothing like their parents at all. A frog lays eggs in water, and out comes a tadpole: no legs, a long tail, and gills for breathing underwater. Over weeks the tadpole grows back legs, then front legs, the tail shrinks away, and lungs replace the gills. The animal that climbs out is a frog. That change is called metamorphosis.

A butterfly does the same thing even more completely: egg, then a caterpillar that eats and eats, then a hard case, and then a butterfly.

And you are on the first road. A baby is a small human being who grows, gains teeth, learns to walk and talk, and becomes an adult - a slow change, with nothing about the shape of the body starting over.

So compare two young animals by asking one question: does it look like its parent, or must it change shape first?
concepts.example: Choose a frog and a goat. Describe how each one changes from young to adult, in order. Then say which of the two is more like a human baby growing up, and why.

concepts.title: Where Our Materials Come From
concepts.explanation:
You have spent this unit mixing materials and separating them again. Now ask a different question about them: where did they come from before anyone mixed anything?

Every material we use comes from planet Earth. There is nowhere else to get anything.

Some come straight out of the ground. Rock is cut from a quarry and used for building. Metal comes from rocks called ores, dug out of a mine and then heated until the metal runs out of them. Salt is mined out of the ground, or left behind when sea water dries in the sun. Clay is dug from a riverbank and fired into pots and bricks.

Some grow on the Earth. Wood comes from trees, cotton from a plant, wool from a sheep - all of them living things that grew on the Earth, out of Earth's soil and water and air.

And some are made by people out of the first two. Plastic is manufactured from oil, and oil comes from deep underground. Glass is made by melting sand. Cement is made from crushed limestone rock.

So even a plastic bowl or a glass window traces back to the ground. Mining, quarrying and drilling are the work of getting those materials out - and because the Earth holds only so much of each one, the amount is not endless.
concepts.example: Pick three objects near you. For each one, name the material and say where on Earth it came from - dug out of the ground, grown by a living thing, or made by people from something that was.
